newsitem.title: INDIA: India's biggest firm pays taxes after 20 years.
newsitem.headline: India's biggest firm pays taxes after 20 years.

text.p: India's biggest private firm is unlikely to see its profits dented by the payment last week of taxes for the first time in 20 years, analysts said.

The 500 million rupees ($13.95 million) that petrochemicals and textiles giant Reliance Industries Ltd made as advance tax for the fiscal year ending on March 31 was meagre on an estimated profit of 13.8 billion rupees, they said.
"Its absolutely peanuts," said Shankar Sharma, research head at First Global Finance, a Bombay-based brokerage that specialises in foreign institutional business.
"It's no big deal. For any serious investor this doesn't mean anything," he said.
Reliance hasn't paid taxes since going public in 1977 -- consistently ploughing back profits into tax-spared expansion and diversification projects.

The 1996/97 (April-March) budget imposed an effective 12.9 percent minimum alternate tax (MAT) on all firms that made profits, but Reliance did not provide for tax in the first six months to September 30, 1996.

"The company's strategy is still not very clear since the amount of tax paid is only 28 percent of our projected tax payout this year," said Nandini Krishnaswamy, Reliance analyst at securities firm Caspian Research India.
She estimated a tax outgo of 1.78 billion rupees on forecasted pre-tax profit of 13.84 billion rupees in the year to March 31, 1997 against 13.05 billion a year ago.
Tax experts said the advance tax due by March 15 usually reflected "the near total" payment.
"The jury is still out on how much it actually ends up paying," Sharma said. "This might be a one-time payment."
The government diluted MAT in the 1997/98 budget on February 28 by exempting export profits from its purview and said firms can adjust it against future tax liability.
Analysts estimate the effective MAT to shrink to 10.5 percent in 1997/98 from 12.9 percent currently.

Reliance officials reached by Reuters would not comment on the tax liability. "I can only confirm that we have made an advance tax payment of 500 million rupees," a company spokesman said. "I have no other details."
Another official said the firm paid other levies.
"We have contributed 127 billion rupees to the government by way of excise, customs and other levies in the past 16 years -- from 740 million in 1980 to 22.34 billion in 1996/97," the official said.
Reliance makes textiles and every raw material -- petrochemicals -- that goes into it.

The company said it is raising total volume output to 6.2 million tonnes in 1997/98 and to 9.3 million tonnes by 1999 from 1.6 million tonnes in 1995/96, making it one of the ten largest petrochemical firms in the world.
It has more than 2.6 million shareholders and a market capitalisation of 3.6 billion rupees and analysts recommend buying the stock.
Reliance is currently trading at a price-earnings multiple of 9.15 on its 1997/98 estimated earnings, Caspian's Krishnaswamy said.
"With earnings expected to grow 28.91 percent in FY98, we believe that this stock will trade at a premium to the market and our 12-month price target is 320 rupees," she said.
The share closed at 279 on the Bombay exchange last week.
